Take any positive integer. If it is even, divide it by 2; if it is odd, triple it and add 1. Repeat this process on the result, over and over. The (still unproven) Collatz conjecture claims that no matter which positive integer you start from, this process will always eventually:
choices: Enter a different cycle depending on the starting number, never settling on the same one
Increase without bound, growing larger forever

questions.q: Buses in a city are scheduled to run every 10 minutes on average, but due to traffic, the actual gaps between consecutive buses vary randomly (sometimes 2 minutes, sometimes 18, etc.), while still averaging 10 minutes overall. If you arrive at the stop at a completely random moment, is your expected wait for the next bus exactly 5 minutes, less than 5 minutes, or more than 5 minutes?
choices: It is impossible to say anything about the expected wait without knowing the exact schedule
Exactly 5 minutes, since half of 10 minutes is always the average wait
More than 5 minutes, because arriving at a random moment makes you more likely to land inside one of the longer gaps
Less than 5 minutes, because buses that are late tend to catch up afterward

Class A has 10 students who averaged 60 on a test. Class B has 40 students who averaged 90 on the same test. Someone claims that combining both classes must give an overall average of exactly 75, the midpoint between 60 and 90. What is the actual combined average, and why?
choices: 75 — the midpoint is always correct when combining two averages
84 — the true weighted average is pulled toward Class B's score because it has four times as many students
90 — the larger class's average always determines the combined average entirely
It cannot be determined without knowing each student's individual score

questions.q: A university reports that its average class size, computed by averaging over all classes, is exactly 20 students. However, when individual students are surveyed and asked how many students are in their classes, the average class size they report comes out noticeably higher than 20. Both figures are computed correctly. How is this possible?
choices: It isn't possible — both averages must be identical if computed correctly
Students in large classes systematically lie about their class size
The university made an arithmetic error in one of the two calculations
Averaging per student over-weights large classes, since each of their many students reports that same large size, while small classes contribute only a few reports each

In the general population, having disease A and having disease B are completely statistically independent. A certain hospital admits only patients who have at least one of the two diseases (A, B, or both). Among only the patients admitted to this hospital, researchers find that having disease A makes it LESS likely a patient also has disease B, even though the diseases are independent in the general population. What explains this?
choices: The hospital's sample size is too small to draw any real conclusion
This is impossible — truly independent traits cannot appear correlated in any subgroup
Disease A must be biologically protective against disease B
Berkson's paradox: conditioning on being admitted (having A or B) induces a spurious negative correlation between the independent causes of admission

A basketball player has an independent 75% chance of making any given free throw, unaffected by prior makes or misses, and has just made 9 in a row. Commentators say he's 'heating up' and is now more likely than usual to make the next one. What is the actual probability he makes his 10th free throw?
choices: It depends on how many more shots remain in the game
Lower than 75%, because streaks must break
Higher than 75%, because he's in the zone
